items.misconceptions: ignores the turn that "though" signals; misreads "costly" as low pay; confuses this turn with the one in line 22

why.B: Explaining how fast the riders traveled is what the paragraph before it does (lines 9–15); “though” signals a turn away from speed.
why.C: Showing that the riders were paid very little misreads “costly”: the passage gives the high price of sending a letter (lines 16–18), and the riders' pay is never mentioned.
why.D: Introducing the telegraph is the job of line 22, “Meanwhile, another kind of messenger was on its way,” not of line 16.

choices.A: small practice paintings

items.explanation: Seurat made smaller drawings and painted studies first, working out where each figure should go, so his studies were small practice paintings for planning the big one.

why.B: Rooms where artists work are studios; Seurat's studies were things he painted (line 19), not places.
why.C: Careful looks at something is what a study means in “a study of the night sky”; here “painted studies” are pictures Seurat made to plan the big one (lines 18–20).

items.subject: RC
items.subskill: main idea — the central idea of the whole passage
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Zinc yellow paint always turns a dull brown.
choices.B: Most painters mix their colors on a palette before painting.
choices.C: Seurat painted with dots of color that mix in the viewer's eye.
choices.D: The painting shows a crowded Sunday on the banks of the River Seine.

items.explanation: The passage explains how Seurat's painting is made of small touches of unmixed color that seem to fall apart up close and come together from a distance; the other choices are single details, and one of them stretches its detail beyond what the passage says.
items.misconceptions: takes the subject of the painting, the usual method or the color change for the whole

why.A: Zinc yellow paint always turning a dull brown stretches one detail from lines 25–27: the passage says only that the zinc yellow in this painting turned brown, not that all zinc yellow does, and one detail is not the main idea.
why.B: Painters mixing colors on a palette is the usual method Seurat turned away from (lines 10–11), background for the main idea rather than the main idea.
why.D: A crowded Sunday on the banks of the River Seine is what the painting shows (lines 5–7), not what the passage mainly explains about it.

choices.A: the sunlit grass
choices.B: the people's faces
choices.C: the monkey's leash
choices.D: the waters of the River Seine

items.explanation: Lines 25–26 say that for the sunlit grass, Seurat used a bright paint called zinc yellow.
items.misconceptions: grabs another painted detail from the passage

why.B: The people's faces are among the things that break into dots up close (line 2), but no paint color is named for them.
why.C: The monkey's leash belongs to a figure Seurat added later (lines 20–22); zinc yellow was used for the sunlit grass.
why.D: The waters of the River Seine come from the setting in line 6, where the crowd gathers on the river's banks; the passage names zinc yellow only for the sunlit grass (lines 25–26).

items.subject: RC
items.subskill: inference — a conclusion the facts support
items.prompt: It can be inferred that people who saw the painting in 1886 saw grass that looked

choices.A: darker than it looks now
choices.B: brighter than it looks now
choices.C: already a dull shade of brown
choices.D: the same as it does in the museum today

items.explanation: Seurat painted the sunlit grass with a bright zinc yellow that by 1892 was turning a dull brown, so visitors in 1886, before the change, saw brighter grass than visitors see today.
items.misconceptions: reverses the direction of the change; dates the change too early; ignores it

why.A: Darker than it looks now reverses the change: the zinc yellow has darkened since then (lines 25–29), so the grass was brighter in 1886.
why.C: Already a dull shade of brown puts the change too early: people noticed the yellow turning brown by 1892 (lines 26–27), years after the painting was first shown.
why.D: The same as it does in the museum today ignores lines 25–29: the yellow has turned brown, so the painting is darker in places than when it was finished.

items.prompt: The word “Sadly” in line 25 shows that the author

choices.A: wishes the colors had not changed
choices.B: believes Seurat was a careless painter
choices.C: is sorry that the painting is in Chicago
choices.D: thinks the painting should be thrown away

items.explanation: “Sadly” comes just before the news that not every color has lasted, so it shows the author is sorry that the bright yellow has turned brown.
items.misconceptions: attaches "Sadly" to the wrong fact; turns regret into blame or rejection

why.B: Believing Seurat was a careless painter does not fit; the author blames nothing on Seurat and says only that one paint he used turned brown (lines 25–27).
why.C: Being sorry that the painting is in Chicago attaches “Sadly” to the wrong fact; it introduces the colors that have not lasted (line 25), not where the painting hangs.
why.D: Thinking the painting should be thrown away goes far beyond “Sadly”; the author describes visitors still enjoying it today (lines 30–31).

items.prompt: The passage provides information to answer which question?

choices.A: Who taught Seurat to paint with dots?
choices.B: Why did Seurat add a monkey on a leash?
choices.C: What did the museum pay for the painting?

items.explanation: Line 8 says Seurat began the painting in 1884. The passage never says who taught him, why he added the monkey, or what the museum paid.

why.A: Who taught Seurat to paint with dots is never said; the passage says only that his way of painting came to be called pointillism (lines 16–17).
why.B: Why Seurat added a monkey on a leash is not explained; lines 20–22 say only that he added new figures, including the monkey.
why.C: What the museum paid for the painting is never mentioned; the passage says only that it hangs in the Art Institute of Chicago today (lines 28–29).

items.subject: RC
items.subskill: main idea — the theme of a story
items.prompt: Which best states a theme of the story?

choices.A: Hard work always earns a fair reward in the end.
choices.B: Storms do more damage than long periods of calm.
choices.C: It is unwise to argue with people who are powerful.
choices.D: Whoever claims to own something must also accept its troubles.

items.explanation: Tamsin shows the lord that if the wind is his property, its idle weeks and its storm damage are his too; once he sees that owning the wind means paying for its harm, he gives up his claim.
items.misconceptions: takes a literal comparison of two events for a theme; reverses Tamsin's success; reaches for a stock moral

why.A: Hard work always earning a fair reward does not fit; Tamsin wins with a clever argument, not with extra work, and no one is rewarded for working.
why.B: Storms doing more damage than calm weeks compares two events in the story (lines 15–17 and 24–25) instead of stating a lesson about them.
why.C: Arguing with the powerful being unwise is the opposite of what happens: Tamsin argues politely with the lord and wins (lines 28–34).

items.prompt: In the story, Tamsin does all of the following EXCEPT

choices.A: pay the weekly sack of flour
choices.B: keep a record on the mill door
choices.C: ask the other millers to join her
choices.D: climb the hill with a bill for the repairs

items.explanation: Tamsin pays like the others, keeps chalk marks on the door, and carries a bill up to the castle, but she never asks the other millers for help; she acts on her own.
items.misconceptions: assumes the hero gathers helpers; skims for the missing action instead of checking each one

why.A: Paying the weekly sack of flour is something she does: line 11 says she paid too and said nothing.
why.B: Keeping a record on the mill door is something she does: each evening she made a chalk mark for a windy day or a still one (lines 11–14).
why.D: Climbing the hill with a bill for the repairs is something she does after the storm (lines 26–28).

items.subskill: vocabulary in context — the meaning of a phrase
items.prompt: In lines 22–23, “could hardly argue” means that the lord

choices.A: argued only a little
choices.B: had no good reason to object
choices.C: agreed to give her more flour
choices.D: was much too angry to say anything

items.explanation: “Could hardly argue” means there was almost nothing he could say against her: by his own rule the wind was his, and it had not come to work, so he had no good reason to object.
items.misconceptions: reads "hardly" as "a little"; reads the frown as speechless anger

why.A: Argued only a little reads “hardly” as “a small amount”; the phrase means he had almost nothing to argue with, since it was his own wind that had not worked.
why.C: Agreeing to give her more flour is never suggested; the lord only frowns at the empty sack and lets the matter drop (lines 22–23).
why.D: Being much too angry to say anything comes from the frown in line 22, but the phrase is about having no good argument, not about being too upset to talk.

items.subskill: inference — a character's reason for acting
items.prompt: Tamsin most likely made a chalk mark on the mill door each evening in order to

choices.A: decorate the door with a pattern
choices.B: count the sacks she owed the lord
choices.C: help her family remember to shut the mill
choices.D: keep proof of the days the wind failed to blow

items.explanation: Tamsin marked each still day with a circle, and when the calm came she pointed to the row of circles to show the servant that the lord's wind had not worked. The marks were her proof.
items.misconceptions: reads the marks as decoration or as a tally of the payments

why.A: Decorating the door takes the marks for a pattern; each one stood for a windy day or a still one (lines 12–14), and she later used them as proof (line 19).
why.B: Counting the sacks she owed the lord mixes the marks up with the payments; a line meant a windy day and a circle a still one (lines 12–14).
why.C: Helping her family remember to shut the mill is never mentioned; the marks recorded the weather, which she pointed to when the servant came (lines 17–19).

items.subject: RC
items.subskill: organization/logic — how two parts relate
items.prompt: How is the summer calm related to the autumn storm?

choices.A: Each shows a problem with owning the wind.
choices.B: Both show that Tamsin's mill was poorly built.
choices.C: The calm hurts the lord, but the storm helps him.
choices.D: The storm happens because of the long summer calm.

items.explanation: In the calm, the lord's wind does no work, so there is no flour to share; in the storm, his wind does damage, so the repair bill is his. Each shows a different trouble that comes with owning the wind.
items.misconceptions: looks for cause and effect between the two events; misjudges whom the storm hurts

why.B: Both showing that Tamsin's mill was poorly built does not fit; no mill turned in the calm (lines 15–17), and the storm was strong enough to flatten a barn.
why.C: The calm hurting the lord but the storm helping him gets the storm backward: it brings him a bill for the repairs (lines 28–30).
why.D: The storm happening because of the calm is never suggested; the two come in different seasons, and the story gives no cause for either.

items.prompt: Which best describes the kind of writing in this passage?

choices.A: a folktale
choices.B: a biography
choices.C: a news report
choices.D: a science article

items.explanation: The story begins “Long ago,” takes place in an unnamed valley, has a clever hero who outwits a greedy lord, and ends by telling what people there still do “to this day,” all marks of a folktale.
items.misconceptions: is misled by the weather in the story or by the line numbers on the page

why.B: A biography tells the true life of a real person; Tamsin and the lord are characters in a tale set “long ago” in an unnamed valley (line 1).
why.C: A news report tells real, recent events with dates and places; this story happens “long ago” and ends with a custom that lasts “to this day” (line 37).
why.D: A science article would explain how wind or storms work; here the wind is the center of a clever argument, not something explained.
